solution.concept_anchor: Potti Sriramulu's pre-fast political identity
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because students link Sriramulu exclusively to the Telugu linguistic movement, assuming his only significant activism was territorial, when in fact his earlier fasts covered social reform issues like temple entry for Harijans.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a) — Sriramulu did not lead the Andhra Pradesh Congress Committee; his fasts were individual acts of conscience, not party leadership roles.
Eliminate option (c) — his activism was not confined to linguistic reorganization; his earlier fasts on temple entry for Harijans distinguish him as a broader Gandhian activist.
Eliminate option (d) — 'Amarajivi' means Immortal Soul, conferred posthumously as a mark of martyrdom, not a title he held during his lifetime for party service.
Confirm option (b) — his reputation as a Gandhian social reformer who had earlier fasted for temple entry of Harijans is the fact that sets him apart from purely linguistic agitationists.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits students' tendency to remember Sriramulu only through the lens of the Andhra statehood movement. Because the 1952 fast is so prominent, many students assume his entire political career was linguistic in nature. In reality, his credentials included Gandhian social reform work — particularly fasting for temple entry rights of Harijans — which gave him moral authority independent of the linguistic cause. A student relying only on his linguistic identity will choose the option about Congress leadership or Telugu activism, missing the social reform dimension entirely.
solution.final_explanation:
Potti Sriramulu is remembered primarily as the martyr of the Telugu linguistic movement, but his political identity was rooted in Gandhian methods and extended well beyond territorial demands. Before the 1952 fast, he had undertaken fasts on social reform issues, including temple entry rights for Harijans — placing him squarely in the tradition of conscience-driven Gandhian activism rather than party-political agitation.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Sriramulu held no formal leadership position in the Andhra Pradesh Congress Committee; his fasts were acts of individual moral pressure, not organisational authority.
• Option (b): Correct. He is distinguished from other linguistic agitationists precisely because his activism pre-dated and transcended the linguistic question — the temple entry fasts are his defining pre-1952 identity marker.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Framing him as a purely linguistic activist ignores the Harijan temple entry fasts — a common exam misconception.
• Option (d): Incorrect. 'Amarajivi' (Immortal Soul) was an honorific conferred posthumously by the Telugu people after his death in 1952, not a title reflecting lifetime Congress service.

Value Addition:
• Sriramulu's Gandhian credentials made it politically awkward for Nehru to dismiss the fast as anti-national agitation.
• His non-affiliation with any party during the fast gave the movement a moral, non-partisan character.
• 'Amarajivi' is the epithet most tested by UPSC — remember it means 'Immortal Soul,' not 'martyr of language.'

solution.concept_anchor: Sriramulu fast 1952 — timeline and causal sequence

statement_analysis.statement: Potti Sriramulu commenced his fast unto death on October 19, 1952, and died after 58 days on December 15, 1952.
statement_analysis.reason: These dates are precisely documented: fast began October 19, death occurred December 15, 1952 — a duration of 58 days.

statement_analysis.statement: Nehru announced the formation of a separate Andhra state immediately upon Sriramulu's death on December 15, 1952.
statement_analysis.reason: The announcement came on December 19, 1952 — four days after Sriramulu's death on December 15; it was not an immediate same-day announcement.

statement_analysis.statement: The violence and riots that erupted in the Andhra region following Sriramulu's death played a decisive role in compelling the government to concede the statehood demand.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-death riots and public unrest across Andhra districts were the proximate political pressure that forced Nehru's hand, since the fast alone had not moved the government during its 58-day duration.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (statements 1 and 3 only) tempts students who correctly identify Statement 2 as wrong but fail to notice that Nehru announced on December 19 not December 15 — they may assume 'immediately' is approximately correct and thus accept Statement 2 as true.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — October 19 start, December 15 death, 58 days: all three figures are consistent and factually established. Statement 1 is correct.
Test Statement 2 — 'immediately upon death' implies December 15 announcement; Nehru's announcement was December 19, four days later. The qualifier 'immediately' makes Statement 2 incorrect.
Verify Statement 3 — riots and violence after Sriramulu's death are historically documented as the direct pressure that moved Nehru; this is correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 2 is the word 'immediately.' A student who knows that Sriramulu's death caused the Andhra announcement may not remember the four-day gap and will accept 'immediately' as essentially true. This is a classic scope-extension trap: the causal link is real, but the temporal precision ('immediately') is false. The correct answer requires knowing not just that Nehru announced the state formation as a consequence of the death, but that the announcement came on December 19 — four days later — after riots made the political situation untenable.
solution.final_explanation:
The 1952 fast is one of the most precisely tested events in post-independence history. The dates and causal sequence are examination favourites.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Sriramulu began his fast on October 19, 1952. He died on December 15, 1952, after 58 days — all three figures are historically verified.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Nehru did not announce the formation of Andhra state on December 15. The announcement came on December 19, 1952 — four days after Sriramulu's death — after widespread rioting across Andhra districts had made inaction politically impossible. 'Immediately' is a false qualifier.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The riots following the death were crucial. The fast alone had not moved the government during 58 days; it was the public disorder after December 15 that constituted the immediate political trigger for Nehru's announcement.

Value Addition:
• Andhra state was formally established on October 1, 1953 — nearly ten months after the announcement.
• Kurnool, not Hyderabad or Madras, was the first capital of Andhra State (1953).
• The four-day gap between death (Dec 15) and announcement (Dec 19) is a frequently tested precision point.

solution.concept_anchor: Nehru's contradictory positions on linguistic reorganization

statement_analysis.statement: Nehru consistently opposed linguistic reorganization of states both before and after independence, viewing it as a threat to national unity throughout his political career.
statement_analysis.reason: Nehru's position was not consistent — he and the Congress supported linguistic reorganization in the pre-independence period (as at the 1920 Nagpur session), and reversed course after 1947 due to fears of fissiparous tendencies; calling his stance 'consistent' is factually wrong.

statement_analysis.statement: Nehru described linguistic reorganization as a 'virus' and 'poison' for national integration, reflecting his post-independence administrative caution.
statement_analysis.reason: This remark is historically documented — Nehru used the terms 'virus' and 'poison' in the post-independence period to express his apprehension about the consequences of language-based state formation.

statement_analysis.statement: The Congress party at its 1920 Nagpur session had reorganized its own provincial committees on linguistic lines, lending an organisational precedent to the demand for linguistic states.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1920 Nagpur session is well-established as the point at which Congress reorganized its provincial committees on linguistic principles, which gave institutional legitimacy to later demands for linguistically organized states.

solution.strong_distractor: b — A student who correctly identifies Statement 1 as incorrect may also incorrectly flag Statement 2 as not correct, confusing the 'virus and poison' remark as an exaggeration or fabrication, leading them to choose option (b) instead of (a).
elimination_logic: Assess Statement 1 — 'consistently opposed throughout his career' is the critical phrase; Nehru supported linguistic reorganization pre-independence (Nagpur 1920 Congress). This makes Statement 1 incorrect.
Assess Statement 2 — 'virus' and 'poison' are Nehru's documented post-independence remarks about linguistic reorganization; Statement 2 is factually correct, so it is NOT the incorrect one.
Assess Statement 3 — the 1920 Nagpur session reorganizing Congress on linguistic lines is a well-documented historical fact; Statement 3 is correct, so it is NOT the incorrect one.
Only Statement 1 is incorrect — select option (a): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here is the word 'consistently.' Nehru's opposition to linguistic reorganization is well-known from his post-1947 statements ('virus,' 'poison'), and many students assume this opposition was his lifelong position. The critical knowledge gap is that pre-independence Congress — including Nehru — actually endorsed linguistic reorganization as a tool for democratic mobilisation (Nagpur 1920). The 'consistent' qualifier converts a half-true statement into a fully false one. Students who only recall his post-independence stance will mark Statement 1 as correct, leading them to the wrong answer.
solution.final_explanation:
Nehru's relationship with linguistic reorganization underwent a fundamental transformation between the pre- and post-independence periods — a contradiction that is central to understanding the Andhra agitation.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Nehru did not consistently oppose linguistic reorganization. Pre-independence, the Congress (including Nehru) supported it — the 1920 Nagpur session reorganized Congress's own provincial structure on linguistic lines. Post-1947, Nehru reversed course, fearing that language-based states would encourage fissiparous tendencies.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Nehru's 'virus' and 'poison' description of linguistic reorganization is a documented post-independence remark, reflecting his administrative caution after the trauma of Partition.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 1920 Nagpur session is the foundational moment when Congress reorganized itself linguistically, creating Andhra Pradesh Congress Committee separately — which later provided organisational infrastructure for the statehood demand.

Value Addition:
• The JVP Committee (1949) similarly cautioned against immediate linguistic reorganization but left a political escape clause.
• Ambedkar also opposed language-based reorganization, preferring smaller administrative states.
• Nehru's pre-independence support for linguistic organisation is often called 'the Congress commitment' that agitators like Sriramulu held the government to.

solution.concept_anchor: Andhra State formation — legal mechanism and timeline

statement_analysis.statement: Nehru announced the intention to form Andhra state on December 19, 1952 — four days after Potti Sriramulu's death.
statement_analysis.reason: December 19, 1952 is the documented date of Nehru's announcement, four days after Sriramulu's death on December 15.

statement_analysis.statement: Andhra State was formally established on October 1, 1953, with Kurnool as its first capital.
statement_analysis.reason: Andhra State came into existence on October 1, 1953, carved out of Madras State, and Kurnool — not Madras or Hyderabad — was designated its first capital.

statement_analysis.statement: Andhra State (1953) was created under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, which Parliament passed specifically to address the Andhra demand.
statement_analysis.reason: Andhra State was created in 1953 through Article 3 of the Constitution — it predated the States Reorganisation Act 1956 by three years; the SRA 1956 actually merged it with Telangana to form Andhra Pradesh.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 3 of the Constitution, Parliament can form new states or alter boundaries by a simple majority, without requiring the consent of the concerned state legislature.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 3 requires only a simple majority in Parliament; the concerned state legislature is consulted for its 'views' but its consent is not mandatory — Parliament is not bound by those views.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Only two' tempts students who correctly identify Statement 3 as wrong but also incorrectly doubt Statement 4, believing that state legislature consent is required for redrawing boundaries.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: December 19, 1952 announcement is a verified date — correct.
Statement 2: October 1, 1953 with Kurnool as capital is textbook fact — correct.
Statement 3: The States Reorganisation Act 1956 came three years after Andhra's formation; Andhra was created via Article 3, not the SRA 1956 — incorrect.
Statement 4: Article 3 uses simple majority and state legislature views are advisory only — correct. Three statements (1, 2, 4) are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the core trap: it conflates two related but distinct legal events. Andhra State (1953) and Andhra Pradesh (1956) are commonly confused. Students who know that language-based states emerged from the 1956 Act assume all linguistic state formations happened through it. The precision required is that Andhra State (1953) was formed under Article 3, three years before the SRA 1956 — and the SRA 1956 actually dissolved it by merging it with Telangana to create Andhra Pradesh.
solution.final_explanation:
The Andhra statehood story involves two distinct legal events separated by three years, and confusing them is one of the most common errors in this topic.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Nehru's announcement on December 19, 1952 is four days after Sriramulu's death — a precision detail frequently tested.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Andhra State formally came into existence on October 1, 1953, with Kurnool as its capital — chosen because Madras city was excluded and remained with the Tamil-majority Madras State.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: This is the central trap. Andhra State was not a product of the States Reorganisation Act 1956. It was created in 1953 under Article 3 of the Constitution. The SRA 1956 came later and merged Andhra State with Telangana to form Andhra Pradesh.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Article 3 is clear — Parliament needs only a simple majority. State legislatures are consulted but their consent is not binding. This distinguishes Article 3 from constitutional amendments under Article 368.

Value Addition:
• The Andhra State Act 1953 is distinct from the States Reorganisation Act 1956.
• Article 3 has been invoked for every subsequent state formation: Jharkhand, Uttarakhand, Chhattisgarh (2000), Telangana (2014).
• Kurnool → Hyderabad as capital shift happened in 1956 after the Telangana merger.

solution.concept_anchor: Dhar Commission and JVP Committee — composition and findings
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) swaps the primary criteria of the Dhar Commission with a plausible-sounding administrative-language hybrid, tempting students who know the commission rejected language but cannot recall the exact alternative criteria it emphasised.
elimination_logic: Dhar Commission (1948) was appointed by the Constituent Assembly under S.K. Dhar — eliminate any option that attributes it to the cabinet or to JVP.
JVP Committee comprised Nehru, Patel, and Pattabhi Sitaramayya — any option substituting Rajendra Prasad or Ambedkar for one of these is wrong.
The Dhar Commission's key recommendation was to reject language as the primary criterion and favour administrative convenience and financial self-sufficiency — match it with List II item 2.
The JVP 'escape clause' acknowledged strong public sentiment could reopen the question — this matches with List II item 4; confirm option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The most common trap here is substituting a member in the JVP Committee. 'J' is Jawaharlal Nehru, 'V' is Vallabhbhai Patel, and 'P' is Pattabhi Sitaramayya. Many students replace Sitaramayya with Rajendra Prasad or Rajagopalachari. Similarly, confusing the Dhar Commission's mandate (Constituent Assembly) with a cabinet appointment is frequent. The swap of criteria between the two bodies — students attributing the 'escape clause' to Dhar rather than JVP — is another classic error this question exploits.
solution.final_explanation:
The Dhar Commission and the JVP Committee are the two sequential pre-Andhra-agitation inquiries into linguistic reorganization, and their distinctions are critical exam knowledge.

Correct Matches:
• A–2: The Dhar Commission (1948), appointed by the Constituent Assembly under S.K. Dhar, recommended rejecting language as the primary basis for reorganization, emphasising administrative convenience and financial self-sufficiency instead.
• B–1: The JVP Committee (1949) was composed of Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, and Pattabhi Sitaramayya — the acronym derives from their names.
• C–4: The JVP's 'escape clause' — that very strong public sentiment could reopen the linguistic reorganization question — was the political opening that Andhra agitators later exploited.
• D–3: The SRC (Fazl Ali Commission, 1953) was appointed after the Andhra agitation's success made nationwide boundary reorganization politically inevitable.

Trap pairings to watch: Swapping Sitaramayya for Rajendra Prasad in JVP, or attributing the 'escape clause' to the Dhar Commission rather than JVP.

Value Addition:
• Dhar Commission predates JVP — a sequence UPSC tests in chronology questions.
• Both bodies broadly agreed: immediate linguistic reorganization was inadvisable.
• The SRC was directly caused by Andhra's success — it was not a pre-planned comprehensive review.

solution.concept_anchor: SRC appointment caused by Andhra agitation success
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both facts — that the Andhra agitation happened before the SRC and that the SRC was appointed after — may still choose (a) thinking R explains A, missing that the SRC's mandate extended to all states, not just to replicate the Andhra model.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? A states the SRC was appointed in December 1953 as a direct consequence of the Andhra agitation. This is factually correct — the appointment followed Andhra's success.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? R states the SRC was mandated to reorganize only the southern states on linguistic lines. This is factually incorrect — the SRC had a broad national mandate to reorganize ALL state boundaries considering linguistic, administrative, and security criteria.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer must be (c): A is correct but R is incorrect.
Confirm: option (c) — A correct, R incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the scope-limitation in R — 'only the southern states.' Students who recall the Andhra agitation as a southern phenomenon may assume the SRC was set up to address southern linguistic demands specifically. In reality, the SRC had a pan-India mandate covering all state boundaries. A student who does not know the SRC's full scope will accept R as approximately correct and choose option (a), missing the critical difference between a regional and a national mandate.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between the Andhra agitation and the SRC's appointment is a cause-and-effect sequence that UPSC tests both directly and through the assertion-reason format.

Assertion (A) — Correct: The States Reorganisation Commission was indeed appointed in December 1953 as a political consequence of the Andhra agitation's success. The successful use of mass pressure to create a linguistic state made it impossible for the government to deny similar demands from Marathis, Gujaratis, Kannadigas, and others — necessitating a comprehensive national review.

Reason (R) — Incorrect: The SRC was not mandated to reorganize only the southern states. Its mandate was pan-Indian — to examine ALL state boundaries across India with reference to linguistic, administrative, financial, and security considerations. Restricting it to southern states misrepresents the SRC's scope entirely.

Since A is correct but R is factually wrong, the answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• SRC's composition: Fazl Ali (Chairman), H.N. Kunzru, and K.M. Panikkar.
• The SRC submitted its report in 1955, leading to the States Reorganisation Act 1956.
• The SRC considered but rejected a separate Telangana state, recommending merger with Andhra — a decision with long-term consequences.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequence of reorganization commissions and key events 1948–1956
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) places the JVP Committee before the Dhar Commission, which seems plausible to students who recall both from 1948–1949 but cannot remember which came first.
elimination_logic: The Dhar Commission was appointed in 1948 by the Constituent Assembly — it must come first among the commissions.
The JVP Committee was set up in 1949 to reconsider Dhar's findings — it follows Dhar and precedes the Andhra State formation.
Andhra State was formally created on October 1, 1953 — after the December 1952 announcement; it comes after JVP.
The States Reorganisation Act is 1956 — latest in the sequence. Correct order: Dhar Commission → JVP Committee → Andhra State formation → States Reorganisation Act. This is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The subtle trap is between the Dhar Commission (1948) and JVP Committee (1949). Both are pre-independence-era bodies in students' mental maps, and many conflate their years. A student who places JVP before Dhar will select option (c). Additionally, students sometimes place the SRA 1956 before the Andhra State formation, not realising Andhra predated the SRA by three years — making option (d) a common wrong choice.
solution.final_explanation:
This chronology tests precise sequencing across an eight-year period of India's reorganization history.

Correct order: Dhar Commission (1948) → JVP Committee (1949) → Andhra State formation (1953) → States Reorganisation Act (1956).

Why each position:
• Dhar Commission (1948): First formal inquiry, appointed by the Constituent Assembly under S.K. Dhar; recommended against language-based reorganization.
• JVP Committee (1949): Set up to reconsider Dhar's findings in light of popular pressure; broadly agreed with Dhar but left the political 'escape clause.'
• Andhra State (1953): Forced by Sriramulu's death and subsequent riots; announced December 1952, formally established October 1, 1953 — under Article 3, not the SRA.
• States Reorganisation Act (1956): Based on SRC (Fazl Ali) report; reorganized all of India into 14 states and 6 Union Territories.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (a): Places SRA before Andhra — reverses the causal sequence.
• Option (c): Places JVP before Dhar — reverses the chronological order of the two commissions.
• Option (d): Omits the distinction between Andhra State (1953) and Andhra Pradesh (1956).

Value Addition:
• The SRC was appointed in December 1953, the same month Andhra State was fully functional.
• The SRA 1956 came into effect on November 1, 1956 — now observed as Rajyotsava Day in Karnataka.
• Fazl Ali Commission submitted its report in 1955, one year before the Act.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 3 — state legislature views are advisory not binding
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) implies Parliament must wait for state legislature concurrence before proceeding, which sounds constitutionally reasonable and mirrors the federal spirit, but incorrectly attributes a binding veto to the state legislature under Article 3.
elimination_logic: The scenario tests whether Parliament is bound by the views of the concerned state legislature under Article 3 — identify the correct legal position first.
Article 3 requires the President to refer the bill to the state legislature for its 'views'; the word 'views' is not 'consent' — Parliament is not bound.
Eliminate option (a) — a constitutional amendment under Article 368 requiring ratification by states is not the mechanism for state boundary changes; Article 3 requires only a simple majority.

Eliminate options (b) and (c) — both imply the state legislature has a blocking or delaying veto, which Article 3 does not provide. Confirm option (d): Parliament may proceed despite the legislature's objection.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits students' general federal intuition: 'surely a state's legislature must consent to losing territory.' In a genuine federal system, this might be true. But India's Article 3 makes the Union Parliament sovereign over state boundaries, requiring only that the President refer the bill to the state legislature for 'views' — and Parliament is explicitly not bound by those views. Students conflate 'consultation' with 'consent,' leading them to option (b). The Andhra and later Telangana precedents both demonstrate that state assemblies' objections did not prevent Parliamentary action.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the precise constitutional mechanics of state reorganization under Article 3 — one of the most practically important articles in India's quasi-federal structure.

Applicable Principle: Under Article 3 of the Constitution, Parliament has the power to form new states, alter boundaries, and change names. The procedure requires the President to refer the Bill to the concerned state legislature for its 'views.' However, Parliament is NOT bound by those views — it may proceed regardless of the state legislature's position. The passage requires only a simple majority, not a special majority under Article 368.

Mapping to the scenario: The Andhra Pradesh legislature's resolution objecting to bifurcation is constitutionally irrelevant to Parliament's power to proceed. Parliament received the views (satisfying Article 3's procedural requirement) and may enact the bill.

• Option (a): Incorrect — Article 368 with state ratification applies to constitutional amendments, not to state reorganization bills.
• Option (b): Incorrect — 'Concurrence' (binding consent) is not required; only 'views' (advisory consultation) are mandated.
• Option (c): Incorrect — there is no mandatory waiting period specified in Article 3 beyond the reference for views.
• Option (d): Correct — Parliament may proceed after receiving views, even if those views express opposition.

Value Addition:
• Article 3 bills are introduced only on the President's recommendation.
• Telangana's creation in 2014 proceeded despite Andhra Pradesh Assembly's opposition — a live example of this principle.
• Article 4 provides that laws made under Article 3 are not to be deemed constitutional amendments.

(b) Parliament must secure the concurrence of the state legislature before enacting the Bill, as the state's objection creates a constitutional bar under Article 3.
(c) Parliament may proceed only after the state legislature is given a fresh opportunity to revise its resolution within a stipulated time period.
(d) Parliament may proceed to pass the Bill by a simple majority, as the state legislature's views under Article 3 are advisory and not binding on Parliament.

solution.concept_anchor: SRC recommendations vs. government deviations
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) regarding Bombay tempts students who know the SRC recommended Maharashtra-Bombay merger; they may assume the government accepted this and kept separate Bombay city as an SRC recommendation rather than a deviation from it.
elimination_logic: Identify which outcome was actually in line with SRC recommendations and which was a government deviation from those recommendations.
The dissolution of Hyderabad State and merger of Telugu areas into Andhra was recommended by SRC — this was implemented; NOT a deviation.
Kannada areas of Hyderabad going to Mysore — SRC recommended this; implemented as recommended.

The retention of Bombay as a separate bilingual state was a government deviation FROM the SRC's recommendation that Bombay merge with Maharashtra. This is the odd one out — an outcome that contradicts SRC's recommendation, unlike the others which followed it. Select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap conflates 'what SRC recommended' with 'what the government did.' Students know Bombay was kept separate and may assume this was part of the SRC's design. In reality, the SRC recommended merging Bombay with the Marathi-speaking state. The government overrode this recommendation and kept Bombay as a separate bilingual state — precisely the deviation that triggered the Samyukta Maharashtra agitation. A student who does not know the SRC's actual Bombay recommendation will treat option (b) as consistent with SRC rather than as the deviation.
solution.final_explanation:
The States Reorganisation Act 1956 implemented most but not all of the SRC's recommendations — and knowing the deviations is as important as knowing the recommendations.

• Option (a): Dissolution of Hyderabad State and merger of its Telugu-speaking areas with Andhra State — this followed the SRC's recommendation. Not the odd one out.
• Option (b): Retention of Bombay as a separate bilingual state — this was a government DEVIATION from SRC's recommendation. The SRC had recommended merging Bombay with the Marathi-speaking areas into a unified Maharashtra. The government's deviation kept Bombay separate, triggering the Samyukta Maharashtra agitation. This is the odd one out.
• Option (c): Kannada-speaking areas of Hyderabad merging with Mysore — SRC recommended this; it was implemented as recommended. Not the odd one out.
• Option (d): Marathwada region of Hyderabad merging with Bombay State — this too followed SRC's recommendation regarding the Marathi-speaking Marathwada region. Not the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• The Samyukta Maharashtra agitation (1956–60) resulted in over 105 deaths in police firing before Maharashtra was formed in 1960.
• The SRA 1956 created 14 states and 6 Union Territories.
• Punjab's bifurcation into Punjab and Haryana came only in 1966 — another deviation from SRC's recommendation to retain a bilingual Punjab.

solution.concept_anchor: Andhra capital history — Kurnool to Hyderabad transition

statement_analysis.statement: Hyderabad was the capital of Andhra State from the time of its formation in 1953 until Andhra Pradesh was formed in 1956.
statement_analysis.reason: Kurnool — not Hyderabad — was the capital of Andhra State (1953–1956). Hyderabad became the capital only after the merger with Telangana formed Andhra Pradesh on November 1, 1956.

statement_analysis.statement: Kurnool was chosen as the first capital of Andhra State partly because Madras city was excluded from the new state and remained with the Madras State.
statement_analysis.reason: Kurnool was selected as the interim capital of the newly formed Andhra State because the Telugu activists' preferred capital — Madras city — was retained by the Madras State due to Tamil leaders' opposition; Kurnool was chosen as a practical alternative.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Kurnool was the first capital may believe Statement 1 is correct 'in spirit' because Hyderabad was always associated with Telugu political identity, and may mark Statement 2 as incorrect because they confuse the reason for Kurnool's selection with administrative factors rather than the exclusion of Madras.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: Was Hyderabad the capital of Andhra State from 1953? No — Kurnool was the capital from 1953 to 1956. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Test Statement 2: Was Kurnool chosen because Madras was excluded? Yes — Madras city remained with the Madras State, and Kurnool was the practical capital choice. Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the near-universal assumption that Hyderabad has always been the capital of Andhra. Because Hyderabad is today the prominent city and was eventually the capital, students project this backwards and assume it was always the capital. The three-year Kurnool interlude (1953–1956) is precisely the fact that distinguishes deep knowledge from superficial familiarity. The reason for Kurnool's selection — Madras city's exclusion — adds a second layer of precision that tests knowledge of the inter-linguistic tension within the Madras State context.
solution.final_explanation:
The capital history of Andhra State and Andhra Pradesh contains one of the most frequently missed facts in this topic.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Hyderabad was NOT the capital of Andhra State (1953–1956). Kurnool served as the capital of Andhra State from its formation on October 1, 1953. Hyderabad became the capital only after the merger of Andhra State with the Telangana region of the former Hyderabad State created Andhra Pradesh on November 1, 1956.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Kurnool's selection as capital was a practical consequence of the exclusion of Madras city. Telugu activists had demanded Madras as their capital, but Tamil leaders strongly opposed ceding the city. Madras remained with the Madras State, leaving Andhra State without its preferred capital — Kurnool was chosen as an interim solution.

Value Addition:
• After Telangana's formation in 2014, Hyderabad was declared a joint capital for 10 years (until 2024).
• Amaravati was proposed as the new capital of the residual Andhra Pradesh.
• The capital question — from Kurnool to Hyderabad in 1956 and then Amaravati — is a recurring exam theme.

solution.concept_anchor: Andhra agitation was separation from Madras State, not Hyderabad
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'Hyderabad State' is the most common wrong answer because students associate the Telugu-speaking Telangana region with the Andhra demand, not realising that the 1952 fast was specifically about separation from Madras State.
elimination_logic: The fast was about forming a state from the Telugu-speaking districts of the then-existing Madras State — not about merging with Hyderabad.
Hyderabad State contained the Telangana region, which became part of Andhra Pradesh only in 1956 — three years after the fast.
Option (b) 'Bombay State' is geographically irrelevant to the Telugu agitation.
Confirm option (c) 'Madras State' — the Andhra demand was for carving out Telugu districts from Madras State.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who know the broader Andhra–Telangana story often conflate the 1952 fast's immediate demand (separation from Madras State) with the 1956 merger (joining with Hyderabad's Telugu areas). The question is set to catch exactly this error. Sriramulu's fast was entirely about separation from Madras State — Hyderabad's Telangana regions were a separate matter resolved three years later through the SRC process.
solution.final_explanation:
Potti Sriramulu's 1952 fast unto death was directed at a precise territorial demand: carving out Telugu-speaking districts from Madras State to form a separate Andhra State.

• Option (a) 'Central Provinces': Incorrect — no Telugu-speaking districts were part of Central Provinces; this is a geographic fabrication.
• Option (b) 'Bombay State': Incorrect — Bombay State had Marathi and Gujarati-speaking populations; Telugu districts were not part of it.
• Option (c) 'Madras State': Correct — the Telugu-speaking districts of Madras State (not Hyderabad) formed the core demand of Sriramulu's fast. Andhra State was carved from Madras State in 1953.
• Option (d) 'Hyderabad State': Incorrect — Hyderabad State contained the Telangana region, which merged with Andhra State only in 1956 under the SRA to form Andhra Pradesh. This merger came three years after Sriramulu's fast.

Value Addition:
• Madras city itself was also demanded by Telugu activists but remained with Madras State — hence Kurnool became the capital.
• The Andhra agitation is specifically about Madras State separation; the 1956 Hyderabad merger is a distinct subsequent event.
• Tamil resistance to ceding Madras city was a parallel agitation within the same Madras State context.

solution.concept_anchor: Gentlemen's Agreement 1956 — Telangana safeguards
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) pairs the 1956 Gentlemen's Agreement with the guarantee of a separate Telangana legislature, which sounds plausible since Telangana did eventually get a separate state — students who know the outcome may reverse-engineer and assume a legislative guarantee was promised.
elimination_logic: The Gentlemen's Agreement of 1956 was a political compact, not a statutory guarantee — it promised safeguards on representation and funds (Telangana Development Fund), not a separate legislature.
Option (b) — 'guarantee of a separate Telangana legislature' was not part of the 1956 agreement; Telangana legislature came only in 2014.
Option (c) — pairing Mulki Rules with 'language instruction rights' is incorrect; Mulki Rules pertained to local employment preference for Telangana residents.

Option (d) — Andhra Pradesh was formed on November 1, 1956, not November 14, 1956. Confirm option (a): 1956 Gentlemen's Agreement promised political representation safeguards and a dedicated Telangana Development Fund.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in option (b) exploits outcome-based reasoning: students who know Telangana eventually got its own state assume the 1956 agreement must have promised some form of separate governance. The Gentlemen's Agreement did not promise a separate legislature — it promised equitable representation within a unified Andhra Pradesh and financial ring-fencing through the Telangana Development Fund. Conflating the eventual 2014 outcome with the 1956 safeguards is the error this question is designed to catch.
solution.final_explanation:
The Gentlemen's Agreement of 1956 was a critical political compact that made the Andhra–Telangana merger possible — and its perceived violation sparked the later Telangana movement.

• Option (a): Correct — the 1956 Gentlemen's Agreement promised Telangana safeguards on political representation within the new state and a Telangana Development Fund to ensure regional equitable development. This is the accurate characterisation.
• Option (b): Incorrect — the Agreement did not promise a separate Telangana legislature. Telangana's separate legislature came only with statehood in 2014. Attributing a legislative guarantee to 1956 is an anachronism.
• Option (c): Incorrect — Mulki Rules (Rules of Local Candidates) were about preference in government employment for those domiciled in Telangana; they were not about language of instruction in schools.
• Option (d): Incorrect — Andhra Pradesh was formally established on November 1, 1956. November 14 is Children's Day (Nehru's birthday), a common date confused in this period.

Value Addition:
• The perceived violation of the Mulki Rules and the Telangana Development Fund triggered the 1969 Telangana agitation.
• The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act 2014 created Telangana as India's 29th state.
• November 1 is celebrated as Andhra Pradesh Formation Day and also as Karnataka Rajyotsava.

solution.concept_anchor: Sriramulu fast compared to Gandhi's fasts — purpose and precedent

statement_analysis.statement: Gandhi's fasts were directed primarily at communal harmony and moral reform within the independence movement, whereas Sriramulu's 1952 fast was specifically for a territorial-administrative demand — a distinction that made the latter a new model for political pressure.
statement_analysis.reason: Gandhi fasted to address communal violence and moral issues; Sriramulu fasted for linguistic statehood — a territorial demand, establishing a precedent for using fasting to coerce administrative outcomes.

statement_analysis.statement: Sriramulu's success set a precedent that directly influenced the strategies of the Samyukta Maharashtra and Maha Gujarat movements, both of which modelled their agitations partly on the Andhra outcome.
statement_analysis.reason: The success of the Andhra agitation in extracting a statehood concession through mass pressure demonstrated a viable model; subsequent movements like Samyukta Maharashtra explicitly drew on this precedent.

statement_analysis.statement: The 'fast unto death' as a political tool was universally condemned by Indian political leaders after Sriramulu's death as an undemocratic and coercive method incompatible with constitutional governance.
statement_analysis.reason: The 'fast unto death' was not universally condemned — it continued to be used as a political tool in subsequent movements; the 'universal condemnation' claim is an overstatement that does not reflect the actual political response.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students tempted to mark all three as correct may accept Statement 3 as approximately true since there were indeed critiques of the fasting tactic, missing that 'universally condemned' is a scope-extension that makes the statement false.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Gandhi fasted for moral/communal reasons; Sriramulu for territorial demand — this distinction is well-established and Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: Samyukta Maharashtra and Maha Gujarat movements citing Andhra precedent is a documented historical influence — Statement 2 is correct.

Statement 3: 'Universally condemned' is the trap qualifier. Subsequent movements continued to use fasting as a tactic (Anna Hazare in modern times, various regional leaders) — universal condemnation never happened. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, 3 incorrect — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 3 is the absolute qualifier 'universally condemned.' Political criticism of fasting as coercive did exist — Nehru and others expressed discomfort — but the method was never universally rejected. Subsequent movements embraced it. A student who recalls that some leaders criticised the tactic may mark Statement 3 as approximately correct, not catching the 'universally' overstatement. This is a classic scope-extension trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The legacy of Sriramulu's fast operates on two levels: its distinction from Gandhian fasting and its precedent-setting effect on subsequent movements.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Gandhi's fasts targeted communal harmony and moral transformation within the freedom movement. Sriramulu's fast was directed at a specific territorial-administrative demand — linguistic statehood. This shift in the purpose of fasting from moral to political-territorial constituted a new model.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Andhra success in 1952–53 demonstrated that sustained mass agitation could force the Union government's hand on reorganization demands. The Samyukta Maharashtra and Maha Gujarat movements explicitly drew on this demonstrated effectiveness.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The 'universally condemned' qualifier is false. Fasting as a political tool was criticised by some leaders but never universally rejected. Subsequent decades saw repeated use of the fast unto death as a pressure tactic in Indian politics.

Value Addition:
• The Samyukta Maharashtra agitation (1956–60) resulted in Maharashtra's formation on May 1, 1960 — Maharashtra Day.
• Critics argued Sriramulu's death 'weaponised' fasting by making the government appear to reward extremism.
• The distinction between Gandhian fasting (moral) and post-Sriramulu fasting (territorial-administrative) is a recurring UPSC conceptual question.

solution.concept_anchor: Bombay Reorganisation Act 1960 — Maharashtra and Gujarat formation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) attributes Maharashtra and Gujarat's formation to 1956 (the SRA), which is the date most students associate with all post-independence linguistic reorganization, missing that Bombay State continued until 1960.
elimination_logic: The SRC recommended merging Bombay into Maharashtra, but the government retained Bombay as a bilingual state in 1956 — so Maharashtra and Gujarat were NOT formed in 1956.
The Samyukta Maharashtra and Maha Gujarat movements continued agitating through the late 1950s.
The Bombay Reorganisation Act 1960 resolved the dispute — Maharashtra and Gujarat formed on May 1, 1960.
Confirm option (c): May 1, 1960 is the date, not 1956 or any earlier year.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who associate all linguistic reorganization with the States Reorganisation Act 1956 will mark option (a) — 1956. The Bombay exception is precisely the fact they miss: the government deviated from SRC's recommendation and kept Bombay bilingual, which required four more years of agitation and over 105 deaths in police firing before the Bombay Reorganisation Act 1960 resolved the question. The 1956–1960 gap is the critical precision this question tests.
solution.final_explanation:
Maharashtra and Gujarat's formation is a distinct event from the 1956 reorganization — a fact often collapsed by students into a single 1956 story.

• Option (a): 1956, under the States Reorganisation Act — Incorrect. The SRC had recommended merging Bombay with Marathi-speaking areas, but the government deviated and kept Bombay as a separate bilingual state. Maharashtra and Gujarat were NOT formed in 1956.
• Option (b): 1959, under the Bombay State Dissolution Act — Incorrect. No such act existed in 1959; this is a fabricated temporal option.
• Option (c): May 1, 1960, under the Bombay Reorganisation Act — Correct. After years of agitation by the Samyukta Maharashtra Samiti and Maha Gujarat Parishad, and over 105 deaths in police firing, the Bombay Reorganisation Act 1960 bifurcated Bombay State into Maharashtra and Gujarat on May 1, 1960.
• Option (d): 1963, as a result of a presidential proclamation — Incorrect. No presidential proclamation was used; the Bombay Reorganisation Act was a Parliamentary statute.

Value Addition:
• May 1 is celebrated as Maharashtra Day and Gujarat Day.
• Over 105 people died in police firing during Bombay agitation protests (1956–60).
• The Samyukta Maharashtra Samiti was formed in 1956; Maha Gujarat Parishad was its counterpart.

solution.concept_anchor: JVP Committee composition — Pattabhi Sitaramayya not Rajendra Prasad

statement_analysis.statement: The JVP Committee was composed of Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, and Rajendra Prasad, who were tasked with re-examining the Dhar Commission's findings.
statement_analysis.reason: The 'P' in JVP stands for Pattabhi Sitaramayya, not Rajendra Prasad. Rajendra Prasad was India's first President and was not part of this committee.

statement_analysis.statement: The Dhar Commission was appointed by the Provisional Parliament in 1948 to assess whether linguistic considerations should guide state reorganization.
statement_analysis.reason: The Dhar Commission was appointed by the Constituent Assembly (not the Provisional Parliament) in 1948; the distinction between the two bodies is constitutionally significant for this period.

statement_analysis.statement: The JVP Committee's report broadly agreed with the Dhar Commission that linguistic reorganization should not be taken up immediately, but included an acknowledgement that very strong public sentiment could reopen the question.
statement_analysis.reason: Both the agreement with Dhar and the 'escape clause' acknowledging strong public sentiment are documented features of the JVP report — this statement is factually accurate.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the JVP composition is wrong in Statement 1 but are uncertain about the Constituent Assembly vs. Provisional Parliament distinction may accept Statement 2 as correct, marking only Statement 1 as incorrect and choosing option (a) instead of (d).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: 'P' in JVP — test whether it is Rajendra Prasad or Pattabhi Sitaramayya. It is Pattabhi Sitaramayya. Statement 1 is incorrect.

Statement 2: Was Dhar Commission appointed by the Constituent Assembly or the Provisional Parliament? It was the Constituent Assembly — Provisional Parliament is incorrect. Statement 2 is also incorrect.
Statement 3: JVP agreeing with Dhar broadly but leaving an escape clause — this is the factually documented outcome. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are incorrect — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the entity-swap trap: Rajendra Prasad and Pattabhi Sitaramayya are both senior Congress leaders from the same period, and both have names beginning with 'P.' A student who cannot recall the exact 'P' will frequently guess Rajendra Prasad — the more prominent figure. Statement 2 adds a second trap: 'Provisional Parliament' and 'Constituent Assembly' are contemporaneous bodies that students often conflate, though they had distinct functions in 1948.
solution.final_explanation:
The JVP Committee's composition is one of the most tested entity-precision points in this topic.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The JVP Committee comprised Jawaharlal Nehru (J), Vallabhbhai Patel (V), and Pattabhi Sitaramayya (P). Rajendra Prasad was India's first President and was not part of this committee. Substituting Prasad for Sitaramayya is the classic entity-swap error.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Dhar Commission was appointed by the Constituent Assembly in 1948, not the Provisional Parliament. While both bodies existed in this period, the Constituent Assembly commissioned the inquiry into linguistic reorganization specifically.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The JVP report agreed with the Dhar Commission that immediate linguistic reorganization was inadvisable, but crucially included an acknowledgement that very strong popular demand could warrant reconsideration — the 'escape clause' that Andhra agitators later exploited.

Value Addition:
• Pattabhi Sitaramayya was a Congress historian and close associate of Gandhi; he contested the Congress president election against Subhas Bose in 1939.
• The JVP report was submitted in 1949, making it the second formal inquiry after Dhar (1948).
• The 'escape clause' in JVP's report is what gave constitutional legitimacy to subsequent linguistic demands.

solution.concept_anchor: SRC composition — Fazl Ali, Kunzru, Panikkar

statement_analysis.statement: The States Reorganisation Commission (1953) was chaired by Fazl Ali, with H.N. Kunzru and K.M. Panikkar as the other two members.
statement_analysis.reason: The SRC's composition is well-documented: Fazl Ali (Chairman), H.N. Kunzru, and K.M. Panikkar — three members in total.

statement_analysis.statement: The SRC recommended the complete dissolution of Hyderabad State, with its Kannada-speaking areas going to Mysore and its Telugu-speaking areas merging with Andhra State.
statement_analysis.reason: The SRC recommended dissolving Hyderabad State and distributing its territories linguistically: Telugu areas to Andhra, Kannada areas to Mysore, and Marathwada to Bombay — this was implemented in the SRA 1956.

statement_analysis.statement: The SRC recommended creating a separate Telangana state as a distinct unit, rather than merging Telangana with Andhra State.
statement_analysis.reason: The SRC did NOT recommend a separate Telangana state — it recommended merging Telangana with Andhra State to form Andhra Pradesh, albeit with safeguards for Telangana.

statement_analysis.statement: The SRC recommended retaining Punjab as a bilingual state, and the bifurcation of Punjab into Punjab and Haryana came only in 1966 — more than a decade after the SRA.
statement_analysis.reason: The SRC recommended retaining Punjab as a bilingual unit; the actual bifurcation into Punjab and Haryana occurred in 1966 under the Punjab Reorganisation Act — a clear example of the government deviating from SRC's long-term trajectory.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know about the Telangana movement may believe the SRC had initially recommended a separate Telangana (since Telangana eventually became a state), leading them to count Statement 3 as correct and thus marking 'Only two' incorrect ones rather than 'Only one.'
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Fazl Ali, Kunzru, Panikkar — standard textbook composition of SRC; correct.
Statement 2: SRC recommending dissolution of Hyderabad and linguistic distribution of its territories — documented recommendation; correct.
Statement 3: SRC recommending a separate Telangana state — this is the factual fabrication. SRC recommended merger with Andhra, not a separate Telangana. Incorrect.
Statement 4: SRC recommending bilingual Punjab, bifurcated only in 1966 — documented fact; correct. Only Statement 3 is incorrect — select option (a): Only one.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a plausible fabrication: since Telangana ultimately became a separate state in 2014, students may assume the SRC had originally recommended its separation. This reverse-projection of outcomes onto historical recommendations is a characteristic UPSC trap. The SRC specifically recommended merger, not separation — and it was the perceived failure of that merger's safeguards that generated the Telangana movement six decades later.
solution.final_explanation:
The SRC's actual recommendations versus what was eventually implemented are among the most nuanced and tested distinctions in this topic.

• Statement 1 — Correct: SRC composition is Fazl Ali (Chairman), H.N. Kunzru, and K.M. Panikkar — three members, submitted report in 1955.
• Statement 2 — Correct: SRC recommended Hyderabad's complete dissolution — Telugu areas to Andhra, Kannada areas to Mysore, Marathwada to Bombay. This was implemented in the SRA 1956.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The SRC did NOT recommend a separate Telangana. It recommended merging Telangana with Andhra State, with political safeguards — which became the basis of the 1956 Gentlemen's Agreement. A separate Telangana was the demand of subsequent movements, not an SRC recommendation.
• Statement 4 — Correct: SRC recommended a bilingual Punjab. The government accepted this initially; bifurcation into Punjab and Haryana came only in 1966 — another deviation from the SRC's long-term framework.

Value Addition:
• The SRC submitted its report in September 1955; the SRA was enacted in 1956.
• The SRC is also called the Fazl Ali Commission after its chairman.
• Punjab's 1966 bifurcation was linked to the Sikh demand for a Punjabi Suba — a religious-linguistic overlap absent in other cases.

solution.concept_anchor: Congress 1920 linguistic organisation — legitimacy for Andhra demand
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true may jump to option (a) without carefully evaluating the causal link, assuming that because Congress organised linguistically in 1920, this directly caused Nehru's concession in 1952.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? A states Congress's 1920 linguistic organisation created an Andhra Pradesh Congress Committee separately from the Madras PCC, giving legitimacy to the Andhra statehood demand. This is factually correct — the 1920 Nagpur session reorganised Congress provincially on linguistic lines.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? R states Potti Sriramulu's own Congress background made it harder for Nehru to dismiss the Andhra movement as anti-national. This is also factually correct — his Congress credentials gave the movement a legitimate, pro-national character.

Step 3: Does R explain A? R explains why Nehru found it politically difficult to oppose the movement — not why the 1920 organisational structure gave legitimacy to the demand. The causal link in R is about Sriramulu's personal credibility, not the organisational precedent of A. R and A are both true but describe separate dimensions of the same political situation, not a direct causal chain.
Both A and R correct, R does NOT explain A — select option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between Congress's organisational structure and the Andhra demand involves two distinct but complementary facts that do not directly explain each other.

Assertion (A) — Correct: The Congress party, since its 1920 Nagpur session, had organised its provincial committees on linguistic lines. This meant an Andhra Pradesh Congress Committee (APCC) existed separately from the Madras Presidency Congress Committee, giving institutional recognition and infrastructure to the Telugu linguistic identity within the Congress framework — lending organisational legitimacy to the statehood demand.

Reason (R) — Correct: Potti Sriramulu's personal credentials as a longtime Congress member and Gandhian activist made it politically awkward for Nehru to portray the Andhra agitation as anti-national or disruptive. His background within the Congress gave the movement a patriotic legitimacy.

Why R does NOT explain A: A is about the organisational precedent set in 1920 that legitimised the demand institutionally. R is about Sriramulu's individual Congress credentials making opposition politically embarrassing for Nehru. These are parallel supporting factors — not a causal chain where R explains A.

Value Addition:
• The APCC's separate existence since 1920 is a model example of how Congress's pre-independence structure shaped post-independence politics.
• Nehru himself had been part of creating the linguistically organised Congress structure — adding a personal contradiction to his post-1947 resistance.
• The tension between Congress high command and regional Congress committees on the Andhra question prefigures many later centre-state conflicts within the party.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect

solution.concept_anchor: Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act 2014 — Telangana as 29th state
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) citing 2013 tempts students who know the Telangana Bill was introduced and debated over an extended period, confusing the year of Parliamentary proceedings with the year of the Act's passage and state formation.
elimination_logic: Telangana became India's 29th state — the question of which act and year is the precision point.
The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act was passed by Parliament in February 2014.
Telangana formally came into existence on June 2, 2014 — under this Act, not under any earlier legislation.
Confirm option (c): 2014, Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 29th state.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap is between 2013 (when Telangana demand received cabinet approval and was in advanced stages of legislative processing) and 2014 (when the Act was actually passed and Telangana formed). Students who track the political process may associate the 'decision' with 2013, missing that the formal legislative instrument — the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act — and Telangana's formal statehood both belong to 2014.
solution.final_explanation:
Telangana's formation is the contemporary culmination of the contradictions embedded in the 1956 merger of Andhra State and Telangana.

• Option (a): 2012, under the States Reorganisation (Amendment) Act — Incorrect. No such amendment act created Telangana; the mechanism was a standalone state-specific act in 2014.
• Option (b): 2013, following a cabinet resolution — Incorrect. While the Union Cabinet approved Telangana's formation in 2013, the actual legislation was passed in 2014; 'cabinet resolution' is not the legally operative instrument.
• Option (c): 2014, under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act — Correct. The Act was passed in February 2014 and Telangana came into existence on June 2, 2014, as India's 29th state.
• Option (d): 2016, under a Presidential Order following a Supreme Court directive — Incorrect. This is a plausible-fabrication option; no Supreme Court directive created Telangana.

Value Addition:
• June 2 is observed as Telangana Formation Day.
• Hyderabad was designated joint capital of both Telangana and Andhra Pradesh for up to 10 years after 2014.
• The 1969 Telangana agitation and the 2001 Telangana Rashtra Samithi (TRS) formation were the key milestones before the 2014 statehood.

solution.concept_anchor: Arguments for and against linguistic state reorganization

statement_analysis.statement: One of the principal arguments against linguistic reorganization was that language-based states would inevitably develop into separatist entities seeking independence from the Indian Union.
statement_analysis.reason: The fear expressed by Nehru, Dhar, and Ambedkar was of sub-nationalism and fissiparous tendencies — not the inevitability of separatism. 'Inevitably' is an overstatement; the empirical outcome showed linguistic states did not become separatist.

statement_analysis.statement: A key argument in favour of linguistic reorganization was that administrative and democratic participation in one's mother tongue would enhance the efficiency and legitimacy of governance.
statement_analysis.reason: Administrative efficiency and democratic participation in the mother tongue are the standard pro-linguistic-reorganization arguments, as citizens could engage more effectively with governance in their own language.

statement_analysis.statement: Ambedkar's position on state reorganization diverged from Nehru's in that Ambedkar favoured smaller states on administrative grounds, though he specifically opposed purely language-based reorganization.
statement_analysis.reason: Ambedkar supported the idea of smaller, more administratively manageable states but was opposed to using language as the primary criterion for their formation — a nuanced position distinct from Nehru's more general caution.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) 'Statement 2 only' tempts students who incorrectly read Statement 3 as claiming Ambedkar agreed with Nehru's position — missing the important distinction that Ambedkar's administrative rationale for smaller states diverged from Nehru's overall approach.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: 'Inevitably develop into separatist entities' — the fear was of sub-nationalism, not guaranteed separatism. Empirically, linguistic states did not separate. 'Inevitably' makes this incorrect.
Statement 2: Administrative efficiency and mother-tongue democratic participation as arguments for linguistic reorganization — standard textbook argument, correct.

Statement 3: Ambedkar favouring smaller states on administrative grounds but opposing language-based reorganization — this nuanced position is well-documented and distinct from Nehru's position. Correct.
Statements 2 and 3 correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1's trap is the word 'inevitably.' The concern was real — Nehru called it a 'virus' — but the claim of inevitability is historically disproved: India's linguistic states did not become separatist. A student who recalls the genuine fear without noting the absolute qualifier will mark Statement 1 as correct. Statement 3 tests knowledge of Ambedkar's specific position, which differs subtly from Nehru's: Ambedkar wanted smaller states (administrative logic) but not language-based ones — a two-part position that students often simplify to 'Ambedkar opposed linguistic states' without the nuance.
solution.final_explanation:
The debate over linguistic reorganization involved multiple intellectual positions, and knowing the precise arguments — and their limits — is critical for UPSC.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The argument against linguistic reorganization was about sub-nationalism and fissiparous tendencies, not the inevitability of separatism. Using 'inevitably' misrepresents the nature of the concern, and the empirical record (India's linguistic states remained firmly within the Union) disproves inevitability.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The pro-reorganization case rested on administrative efficiency (governance in mother tongue) and democratic legitimacy (citizens participating meaningfully in their own language). This is the standard formulation.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Ambedkar's position was distinctive — he favoured smaller states for administrative manageability but specifically opposed language as the criterion. This is different from Nehru's caution, which was more broadly about national unity rather than state size.

Value Addition:
• India's linguistic federalism is today cited as a successful model in comparative politics — states did not become stepping stones to secession.
• The 'one state one language' principle was not strictly followed — Maharashtra and Goa both retained bilingual provisions.
• Ambedkar's States and Minorities (1945) contains his views on state reorganization.

solution.concept_anchor: Andhra agitation as pro-integration sub-national assertion
solution.strong_distractor: a — The Sikh demand for Punjabi Suba tempts students because it involved a religious dimension (Sikh identity) overlaying the linguistic claim — students may assume this religious overlay makes it 'different' from Andhra, when in fact all four options except (c) were movements seeking specific units within the Indian Union rather than separation from it.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: movements that sought a specific state or administrative unit WITHIN the Indian Union, asserting sub-national identity while accepting the Union framework.
Andhra agitation — sought a Telugu-majority state within India: pro-integration, within the Union framework.
Punjabi Suba demand — sought a Punjabi/Sikh-majority state within India: pro-integration, within the Union framework.

The demand for a separate state of Nagaland by Naga nationalists — this is a secessionist movement, initially seeking independence from India, not merely a distinct unit within the Union. This is the odd one out. Select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap works by grouping sub-national assertions together and asking students to distinguish pro-integration from secessionist movements. The Naga movement initially sought independence — not just a separate state within India — making it categorically different from the Andhra, Punjabi Suba, and Samyukta Maharashtra demands, which all operated within the constitutional framework of the Indian Union. Students who vaguely recall 'Nagaland was formed' may confuse the eventual outcome (statehood within India) with the movement's original secessionist character.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the critical conceptual distinction between legitimate sub-national assertion within a constitutional framework and secessionist movements.

• Option (a): Andhra agitation for a separate Telugu-majority state — explicitly pro-integration. Sriramulu and his supporters wanted to be part of India, just in a Telugu-majority administrative unit. Not the odd one out.
• Option (b): Samyukta Maharashtra movement for a Marathi-majority state — similarly pro-integration, operating entirely within the Indian constitutional framework and eventually resolved through a Parliamentary statute. Not the odd one out.
• Option (c): Naga nationalist demand — this is the odd one out. The Naga movement, particularly in its early phase under the Naga National Council, sought independence from India — not merely a separate state within the Union. This makes it categorically secessionist rather than sub-national assertionist.
• Option (d): Sikh demand for Punjabi Suba — a linguistic-religious demand for a Punjabi/Sikh-majority state within India, eventually granted in 1966. Pro-integration within the Union framework. Not the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• Nagaland became a state within India only in 1963 — after years of insurgency and negotiation; the Naga movement's trajectory from secession to statehood is unique.
• The Andhra, Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Punjabi Suba movements are classified as 'legitimate sub-national assertions within constitutional federalism.'
• The distinction between secessionist and sub-national assertionist movements is a recurring UPSC polity-history crossover theme.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

(a) The Andhra agitation led by Potti Sriramulu for a separate Telugu-majority state
(b) The Samyukta Maharashtra movement for a Marathi-majority state carved out of Bombay State
(c) The early Naga nationalist movement's demand for self-determination separate from the Indian Union
(d) The Sikh community's demand for a Punjabi Suba — a Punjabi-majority state within the Indian federation

solution.concept_anchor: Riots caused announcement — not fast alone; Andhra predates SRA 1956

statement_analysis.statement: Nehru's announcement of Andhra state's formation on December 19, 1952 was primarily a response to the eruption of widespread riots and public disorder in Andhra districts following Sriramulu's death, rather than a change of heart during the 58-day fast itself.
statement_analysis.reason: During the 58-day fast, the government did not concede; it was the post-death riots that constituted the immediate political trigger for Nehru's December 19 announcement — a documented causal sequence.

statement_analysis.statement: Andhra State, formed in 1953, was one of the states constituted under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, which comprehensively reorganized state boundaries across India.
statement_analysis.reason: Andhra State was formed in 1953 — three years before the SRA 1956 — through Article 3 of the Constitution, not the SRA 1956; the SRA 1956 actually merged it with Telangana to create Andhra Pradesh.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may mark both statements as correct if they are unaware of the SRA trap in Statement 2, knowing only that Andhra Pradesh emerged from the 1956 reorganization (confusing Andhra State with Andhra Pradesh).
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: Was it riots after the death (not the fast itself) that triggered Nehru's announcement? Yes — the government remained unmoved during 58 days; it was post-death disorder that forced the hand. Statement 1 is correct.
Test Statement 2: Was Andhra State created under the SRA 1956? No — Andhra State was created in 1953 under Article 3, predating the SRA 1956 by three years. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a precisely constructed temporal-swap trap. Andhra Pradesh (1956) and Andhra State (1953) are two different entities. The SRA 1956 created Andhra Pradesh — but Andhra State had already existed for three years by then. Students who know 'Andhra Pradesh was part of the 1956 reorganization' reverse-project this onto the earlier Andhra State formation and conclude both were SRA products. The question is designed to expose exactly this conflation.
solution.final_explanation:
Two critical precision points about the Andhra agitation's immediate and medium-term outcomes are tested here.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The government did not respond to the fast during its 58-day duration. The political tipping point was the violence and riots that swept Andhra districts after Sriramulu's death on December 15, 1952. Nehru's announcement came on December 19 — driven by the public disorder, not by a change of heart during the fast. This causal precision is essential: the fast created moral pressure; the riots created political urgency.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Andhra State (1953) was created through Article 3 of the Constitution — three years before the States Reorganisation Act 1956. The SRA 1956 did not create Andhra State; it dissolved it by merging it with Telangana to form Andhra Pradesh. Treating Andhra State as an SRA product fundamentally confuses two distinct legal events.

Value Addition:
• Article 3 (not Article 368 or SRA) is the operative mechanism for all state formations, including 2000 and 2014.
• Andhra State existed as a separate entity from October 1, 1953 to October 31, 1956 — a brief three-year existence.
• The SRA 1956 came into effect on November 1, 1956 — the same day Andhra Pradesh was formally created.

solution.concept_anchor: SRA 1956 — 14 states and 6 Union Territories outcome
solution.strong_distractor: c — '15 states and 5 Union Territories' is a plausible fabrication that sounds close to the correct figures, exploiting students' uncertainty about the exact count without a dramatically wrong number.
elimination_logic: The States Reorganisation Act 1956 reorganized India's administrative map — the output was a specific number of states and Union Territories.
The documented outcome is 14 states and 6 Union Territories — this is the standard textbook figure for 1956.
Option (a) '12 states and 8 Union Territories' misrepresents both figures significantly.
Confirm option (b): 14 states and 6 Union Territories.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the substitution of similar-sounding but incorrect numbers. 14 states and 6 Union Territories is the specific output of the SRA 1956 — a figure many students remember approximately but not precisely, making them vulnerable to options that adjust one or both numbers by a small margin. Option (c)'s '15 and 5' is the most dangerous distractor since it differs by only one unit in each category.
solution.final_explanation:
The States Reorganisation Act 1956 transformed India's administrative map in one comprehensive legislative exercise.

• Option (a): 12 states and 8 Union Territories — Incorrect. Both figures are wrong; 12 understates the states and 8 overstates the UTs.
• Option (b): 14 states and 6 Union Territories — Correct. This is the documented outcome of the SRA 1956. The 14 states included Andhra Pradesh (newly formed by merging Andhra State with Telangana), Mysore, Bombay, Kerala (formed by merging Travancore-Cochin with Malabar), and others.
• Option (c): 15 states and 5 Union Territories — Incorrect. The number of states was 14, not 15; UTs were 6, not 5.
• Option (d): 16 states and 4 Union Territories — Incorrect. Further from the correct figures on both counts.

Value Addition:
• Kerala was a notable creation of the SRA 1956 — formed by merging the princely state of Travancore-Cochin with the Malabar district of Madras State.
• The number of states has grown from 14 (1956) to 28 (2019) as of the last reorganization.
• The SRA 1956 did not create Gujarat and Maharashtra — they remained part of Bombay State until 1960.

concepts_used: Role of Madras State in the Andhra Agitation: Territorial and Political Dimensions
Kurnool as First Capital of Andhra State (1953–1956): Significance and Change

solution.concept_anchor: Madras city excluded from Andhra State — remained with Tamil Madras State
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) pairs the demand for Madras city as capital with the claim that it was initially included in Andhra State, which sounds plausible since Telugu activists did demand Madras — students may not recall that the demand was ultimately denied and Madras remained with Madras State.
elimination_logic: The key fact: Tamil leaders strongly opposed ceding Madras city to Andhra, and it ultimately remained with Madras State.
Option (a): Claiming Madras city was the first capital of Andhra State — incorrect; Kurnool was the first capital.
Option (b): Claiming Madras city was 'initially included' in Andhra State — incorrect; it was never included; Telugu demand for Madras was denied.

Option (c): Attributing Tamil opposition to the Andhra statehood concept itself (not specifically to Madras city) — incorrect; Tamil leaders' opposition was specifically about ceding Madras city and certain districts.
Confirm option (d): Telugu linguistic activists demanded Madras city as their capital, Tamil leaders opposed ceding it, and it remained with Madras State — all three facts in this pair are correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap exploits students who know 'Madras was involved in the Andhra agitation' but cannot recall the precise outcome: Madras city was demanded but denied, remaining with the Madras State. Options (a) and (b) are designed to test whether students know that Madras was never part of Andhra State — not even temporarily. The demand existed; the concession did not.
solution.final_explanation:
The Madras city question was one of the most contentious inter-linguistic disputes within the Andhra agitation.

• Option (a): Madras (Chennai) as the first capital of Andhra State — Incorrect. Madras was demanded by Telugu activists but was never part of Andhra State. Kurnool was chosen as the capital precisely because Madras was excluded.
• Option (b): Madras city initially included in Andhra State before being transferred to Tamil Nadu — Incorrect. Madras city was never included in Andhra State at any point; it remained with the Madras State throughout and became the capital of Tamil Nadu when Madras State was renamed.
• Option (c): Tamil leaders supported Andhra statehood but opposed only the inclusion of Madras district (not Madras city) — Incorrect. Tamil leaders opposed ceding both Madras city and certain districts; the city was the most contested element.
• Option (d): Telugu linguistic activists demanded Madras city as the capital of the proposed Andhra state; Tamil opposition to this demand was decisive, and Madras city remained with Madras State — Correct. This accurately captures the demand, the opposition, and the outcome.

Value Addition:
• Madras State was renamed Tamil Nadu in 1969.
• The exclusion of Madras city from Andhra gave Kurnool its brief three-year role as Andhra's capital (1953–1956).
• The inter-linguistic tension over Madras city foreshadowed later disputes like the Cauvery water-sharing controversy.

(b) Madras city — Initially included within Andhra State upon its formation in 1953, before being ceded back to the Madras State under the SRA 1956
(c) Tamil political opposition — Directed at the concept of Andhra statehood itself rather than specifically at the demand to include Madras city in the new state
(d) Madras city — Demanded by Telugu linguistic activists as the capital of the proposed Andhra state but ultimately retained by Madras State due to Tamil opposition, leading to Kurnool's selection as Andhra's first capital
